overview: Welsh is a broad people-and-region label, not the name of one united state in 800-1000. Kingdoms such as Brycheiniog and Gwynedd had their own courts and connections. Excavations reveal fine clothing, farming, trade and commemoration; these regional examples should not become universal Welsh customs.

periods.title: Regional kingdoms
periods.summary: Royal communities and rural settlements developed within several Welsh kingdoms.

periods.title: Courts, crafts and sea contacts
periods.summary: Llan-gors and Llanbedrgoch provide unusually concrete evidence for buildings, clothing and exchange.

periods.title: Later political changes
periods.summary: Welsh princes continued long after the atlas label ends; later English conquests belong to subsequent centuries.

sections.title: A royal island and remarkable sewing

items.text: At Llan-gors Lake, excavations revealed an artificial island associated with the rulers of Brycheiniog. Brushwood and sandstone formed its body, reinforced by oak plank palisades. Creating a royal site required moving ordinary materials in large quantities.

The site was built in the 890s and lasted only briefly before fire. A chronicle records a Mercian attack at the lake in 916, including captives. Connecting that written event with the archaeological burning is plausible, but remains an interpretation.

A charred clothing fragment survived in waterlogged silts beside the island. Conservators separated its fragile layers to reveal birds, vines and lions. What first looked like a burnt lump became evidence of exceptionally skilled needlework.

The base cloth had 23 linen threads per centimetre, decorated with silk and linen. A hem and belt loop suggest a garment, but its full shape and owner are unknown. Calling it definitely a queen’s dress would go further than the evidence.

Llanbedrgoch produced coins and lead weights before major excavation began. Anglo-Saxon coins and Viking-associated weights show contact around the Irish Sea. They do not by themselves prove that everyone at the site came from overseas.

Postholes and other traces revealed halls used around 890-970, with another large building dated broadly 855-1000. These were not stone castles. Archaeologists reconstruct timber structures from the features left in the ground.

Iron leatherworking tools, bucket fittings and household objects came from a deposit of discarded material. The settlement’s life included making, repairing and carrying things as well as political power.

The museum describes crop growing, livestock and crafts alongside contact with merchants. Farming and trade supported one another. Seaborne connections did not mean that dinner arrived entirely by ship.

sections.title: People remembered in bone and stone

items.text: Five people were buried in the filled ditch at Llanbedrgoch during the late 900s. Their unusual treatment has prompted suggestions of violence or captivity. The circumstances are uncertain; Viking contacts do not identify the people responsible.

Researchers made facial reconstructions from four of the skulls. Such models help visitors encounter individual people, but soft tissues and appearance involve estimates. Similar-looking faces are not a DNA-tested family tree.

The tenth-century Conbelin Cross at Margam bears knotwork, Christian figures and a hunting scene. Its Pennant sandstone carving connected religious commemoration with skilled stonework. The person remembered in the inscription is not fully identifiable.

CONBELIN P[O]SUIT HANC CRUCM means “Conbelin erected this cross.” Brackets show a letter restored by the editor. This is Latin in the Conbelin Cross inscription, not Old Welsh; the rest asks for commemoration of a person whose name is damaged.

ending.text: Welsh people did not end in 1000. Regional states and later princedoms continued, facing changing alliances and English conquests in later centuries. Welsh language and identity also continued. The end of the atlas segment is a map boundary, not a people’s extinction or a single conquest date.
